prize_parts.citation: for a visionary, densely patterned body of prose, with its roots in Romanian poetry, in which memory, the body and dream are built into an encyclopedic metaphysical cosmos

statement.case_for: My first choice is unchanged, but I have narrowed the citation after the exchange. The case for Cărtărescu rests on the criteria in the protocol. His voice is distinctive: in the Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy and Solenoid, body, childhood memory, dream and metaphysical speculation form one imaginative system in dense, patterned sentences. His formal and linguistic ambition is sustained across large structures, which are cycles and not isolated books. Imaginative and intellectual depth shows in how a visionary and modernist inheritance is recast as a personal cosmology. The oeuvre runs over several decades and moves between registers, from the intimate and bodily to the cosmic. That bears on maturity. After Mattson's and the chair's questions I would centre the citation on the novels and treat the poetry as the foundation of the project, not an equal pillar, since our coverage of the poetry is thin. A single-writer citation is straightforward. Can Xue remains a very close alternative, and I regard the choice between her and Cărtărescu as a narrow judgment. I do not count first-preference blocs as literary evidence, and I am not moving in order to reach four votes.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and unresolved. The late long volumes may show recurrence of motif as thinning and not as architecture, and I cannot settle that from the supplied evidence. Olsson's question about originality beyond the Romantic and modernist lineage is a real test, and I answer it only partly: the synthesis seems to me his own, but this is a judgment from public knowledge and translation. My assessment is also mediated by translation, and I have not independently verified any text or the quality of the translations. If the committee concluded that the late books restate the early cycle, my first choice would weaken considerably and Can Xue would become the stronger recommendation. The same applies in reverse if her long novels were shown not to match her best short fiction.

responses.point: Mattson holds that Cărtărescu's late books extend the project, with Solenoid widening scale and register, and that the poetry is a foundation of the prose. She has said she would reconsider if the later work were shown to thin.
responses.response: I share her reading of Solenoid as an expansion and not a restatement, but I hold it with the same caution she shows, because I know it through translation. On the citation, the chair asked whether prose and poetry are equal strands. I would not credit the whole body of work with a unity I have seen mainly in the major novels. I would word the citation so that the novels carry the claim and the poetic origins explain its texture. If she can point to specific later volumes where the density clearly deepens, that would strengthen my position. If the committee cannot say, I would not rest the citation on it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Zurita first. He argues that the extra-textual works extend a poetics already present in the books, and that Zurita's sequences are more tightly built than Cărtărescu's longer prose forms. He also asks whether Cărtărescu is original beyond his lineage.
responses.response: I accept his correction on the extra-textual works: they extend a poetics already in the books and do not replace it, and a citation confined to Purgatory and Anteparadise is workable in principle. That makes his case stronger than I treated it in round 1. I still cannot rank Zurita first, because I judge poetry least well in translation and cannot say whether the later volumes keep the early intensity. I would want Spanish-language expert reading before a final recommendation. On tightness, I agree that length does not prove sustained quality. Each section of a cycle must earn its place, and that is the test I apply to the late Cărtărescu volumes. I do not consider the question settled in either direction.

responses.point: Carlberg holds that Can Xue's formal discipline is the work itself, while Cărtărescu's achievement leans more on accumulation and lineage. She names Cărtărescu as her first alternative and says she would not resist a committee reading that rates his long novels higher.
responses.response: Her distinction between discipline and accumulation is the sharpest statement of the difference between our two leading candidates. Where I differ is on how she weighs it. Accumulation across a large structure is also a formal discipline when the parts do real work, and the question is whether the Cărtărescu cycles meet that standard. I admit her point about Can Xue's consistency cuts both ways in my own assessment. A method held that tightly is either a sign of rigour or a limit on range, and I cannot tell which from the supplied description. We share the same translated sample, so our agreement on Can Xue's rigour is not an independent check.

responses.point: Palm argues that the repetition risk costs Can Xue less because her work is more compressed, and that the variety lies in invention within each work and not in a shift of method.
responses.response: That is a fair argument and a real advantage in compactness. If invention within each work is the measure, Can Xue's case is stronger than I credited in round 1. My hesitation is that variety within a fixed method and variety of scale and register are different things, and the citation criterion of sustained quality over a whole oeuvre can be read either way. I also note her point that her own agreement with Carlberg is no check on translation. I accept that and apply it to my own reading of Cărtărescu. If the committee could compare translators' versions of the longer Can Xue novels, it would bear directly on the question she and I both consider open.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Can Xue first. She says a single stable method held with rigour may be a stronger sign of sustained quality than scale alone, and says she would reconsider the order if colleagues could show real variation within the method.
responses.response: I accept the principle that scale alone proves nothing, and I apply it to Cărtărescu. Her stated test is also the right one, and it applies equally to both writers: whether specific later works show real variation within the method or the cycle. I cannot supply that evidence from the supplied files. Her point that opacity could limit significance is one I take seriously for Can Xue. The corresponding risk for Cărtărescu is excess. These are comparable risks and neither settles the comparison, which is why I keep Can Xue as my first alternative and not as a distant second.

uncertainties: Whether Cărtărescu's late long volumes extend the earlier project or restate it cannot be settled from the supplied evidence. I rely on public knowledge and translation and have not independently verified any text.
Coverage of his poetry and earlier fiction is thin, so the claim of unity between poetry and prose is partly inferred. I would therefore centre the citation on the novels.

The comparison with Can Xue is close and could reasonably go the other way. It turns on whether variety of scale and register or rigour of a fixed method is the better sign of sustained quality, and on how well her long novels are translated.
For Zurita, I cannot judge whether the later volumes keep the early intensity, and poetry in translation limits my reading. Spanish-language expert input is not part of the evidence.
Comparing poets, hybrid writers and novelists under common criteria remains imprecise. My judgments of Carson, Adonis and Robinson rest on public reputation and translation.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to any shortlisted writer is documented in my profile, and I request no recusal. My own fiction and essays are set largely in Central Europe, and I have lived in Prague and Vienna. That is context only. It is not evidence of a preference, and Cărtărescu is a Romanian writer I have no recorded connection to. My 2025 public remarks on that year's laureate may reflect a collective position and say nothing about my vote now. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
